tip: '¿Cómo te llamas?' uses the informal 'te' – for friends, family, and people your age.
'Segundo' keeps its full shape before a noun: 'el segundo piso'. Only 'primero' and 'tercero' drop the '-o' there ('primer piso', 'tercer piso') – other ordinals keep it.
'Para' before an infinitive means 'in order to': 'para firmar' = so I can sign. English hides purpose in a bare 'to'; Spanish flags it with 'para'.
Spanish uses 'tener' (to have) for age: 'tiene X años' = is X years old. English uses 'to be' but Spanish literally 'has' years.
'Espero que' flips the verb into subjunctive: 'hayas tenido', not 'has tenido'. A hope isn't a fact, and Spanish stamps that uncertainty right onto the verb.
'Nuevo trabajo' ('nuevo' first) = new-to-me, another one; 'trabajo nuevo' = brand-new. Position slides 'nuevo' between 'different' and 'freshly made'.
'Quiero' here means 'I love' – 'querer' covers both wanting and loving; context decides.
'Despedirse' is reflexive: 'nos despedimos' = we said goodbye. The reflexive marks that the action affects the subject.
No word for 'on': 'el sábado' alone means on Saturday. The article does the work – and 'los sábados' means every Saturday.
'Noticias' is plural – Spanish counts news piece by piece. So today's news 'son buenas': plural noun, plural verb, plural adjective.
Near needs 'de': 'cerca de la playa'. English skips the 'of' (near the beach); Spanish never does – 'cerca de', 'lejos de', always.
Why 'las' in 'a las siete'? Spanish counts the hours: at the seven (hours). Times take the article – 'a la una', 'a las dos', 'a las siete'.
'Tomo' here means 'I drink' – 'tomar' means both 'to take' and 'to drink'. Context makes it clear.
'Before sleeping'? Spanish bans -ing after prepositions. After 'antes de' comes the infinitive: 'antes de dormir', never a gerund.
English drops 'that': she thinks it's a good idea. Spanish never drops 'que' – 'cree que es buena idea'. Skipping 'que' sounds broken.
Subject after the verb: 'empieza el frío' – literally 'starts the cold'. Spanish happily flips the order when the subject is the news.
'El agua' – feminine noun using 'el' for sound: feminine nouns starting with stressed 'a-' take 'el' not 'la' but stay feminine: 'el agua fría'.
'Hermano mayor' isn't the bigger brother – 'mayor' means older. Age uses 'mayor'/'menor', size uses 'grande'/'pequeño'.
'Duermo', not 'dormo': the 'o' swells to 'ue' exactly where stress hits the stem. In 'dormimos' the stress moves to '-i-', so the 'o' survives untouched.
How you do it = 'mal' (adverb); what it is = 'malo' (adjective). 'Duermo muy mal' – sleeping badly, so 'mal'; 'malo' would describe the sleep itself.
One word 'porque' = because; split with accent '¿por qué?' = why. The question uses 'por qué', the answer uses 'porque': 'porque hace frío'.
'Ida y vuelta' – literally 'go and return'.
'Mañana' means both tomorrow and morning. Need both? 'Mañana por la mañana' = tomorrow morning – the article 'la' marks the time-of-day one.
'Ser' + physical traits: 'es alta'. 'Ser' for characteristics seen as defining, not temporary.
'Por poco' + present tense = almost (did something). A near-miss construction.
Location takes 'estar' – except events! Meetings happen, so 'ser': 'la reunión es en la sala tres'. Where things sit = 'estar'; where they take place = 'ser'.
'Estar' for location: the seat 'está' (is located) near the window.
'A primera hora' – at first hour – is Spanish for 'first thing in the morning'; 'para mañana a primera hora' = by early tomorrow.
'Salón' isn't a salon – it's the living room. 'El sofá del salón' = the living-room couch. A hair salon is a 'peluquería'.
One verb means 'to take (time)': 'tardar'. 'El tren tarda treinta minutos' – no extra words needed. Cousin of 'tarde': late.
